extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and novelists (aspiring and intermediate), attendees of The Novelry courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting an effective unreliable narrator in fiction (especially novels/thrillers), covering why to use one and three core rules for making the device believable and narratively rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: The lie needs to have a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a purpose to the unreliability — a reason for it, and the subsequent fallout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreliability should be motivated by plot and character stakes, not gimmickry. Examples: Jo Harding (Close to Me) loses a year of memories after a head injury, which is pivotal to the plot; Gail Frost (The Assistant) lies out of a sense of grievance and entitlement that drives her choices. The lie should create meaningful consequences and narrative fallout that justify its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: The unreliable narrator’s 'truth' is their primary motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: A character’s motivation colors everything they do; the unreliable narrator often fully believes their version of the truth and is driven by that belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out what the narrator wants and how far they'll go to get it; that unshakable certainty should explain discrepancies between facts and interpretation. Use motivation to make lies believable and to seed clues: if the narrator truly believes their version, readers can understand (and forgive) actions even when facts contradict them. The whodunnit structure benefits from this, as readers act as detectives interpreting lies and motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatever the reason, they have no choice (domino effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators are frequently trapped in lies or delusions that grow until continuing the deception becomes the only option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build escalating consequences so one lie leads to another, making reversal impossible without major cost. Example: in Yellowface the narrator keeps resetting moral boundaries until the lie is so large it must be sustained. The sense of being trapped increases tension and inevitability, leading to a satisfying reckoning when truth emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter narrative through the character’s biases — show, don’t tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Present descriptions and observations through the narrator’s unique perspective, highlighting conscious and unconscious bias to reveal unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what matters to the narrator (what they notice, ignore, or misremember) and let that shape sensory detail and emphasis. This technique both builds character and allows readers to infer what the narrator omits or distorts. The page explicitly recommends using the character’s lens to 'show, not tell' and to imbue simple descriptions with the narrator’s unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a plausible cause for the unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the narrator’s unreliability plausible by grounding it in recognizable causes such as memory loss, emotional stress, conscious lying, or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic mechanisms (e.g., blackout from drinking, head injury, self-preservation, delusion, grievance) so readers accept the unreliable perspective. Examples cited: Rachel in The Girl on the Train (alcohol-related memory gaps), memory loss after injury (Close to Me), chronic grievance/resentment (The Assistant). Plausibility helps sustain reader trust in the story even while the narrator misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the story a question or quest the reader wants answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narration is most effective when it creates a central question or mystery that the reader is compelled to solve alongside (or against) the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the narrator’s gaps, lies, or conflicting accounts to withhold key information and set up a quest (e.g., 'what really happened?', 'who is telling the truth?'). Examples: The Girl on the Train (a missing period of memory creates a question), Gone Girl (opposing accounts create competing truths). The eventual emergence of truth should resolve that narrative question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability can trump likability — make the narrator intriguing and complex
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator need not be likable to engage readers; they can be flawed, frustrating, or mysterious and still hold reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the narrator as a puzzle: their flaws and unreliability can be a source of fascination rather than alienation. Craft contradictions and delusions that provoke curiosity and emotional investment, rather than insisting on a sympathetic protagonist. Examples: Barbara Covett (Notes on a Scandal) is creepy yet compelling; flawed narrators can still drive empathy or fascination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unreliable narration to invite the reader to play detective — plant clues and conflicting accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the reader an active interpreter by seeding clues, omissions, and conflicting evidence that reward close reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough factual anchors and discrepancies that attentive readers can piece together or question the truth. Multiple perspectives or opposing accounts (as in Gone Girl) can highlight unreliability and create a richer puzzle. Avoid total obfuscation — the device works best when truth is discoverable and the reader’s detective work is satisfying.
